content: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are recommended as the first-line treatment for children with persistent asthma. While generally considered safe, there is ongoing concern about their potential systemic side effects, particularly their impact on linear growth in children. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of ICS on the linear growth of children with persistent asthma. The review also aimed to identify factors that might modify this effect, such as the specific ICS molecule, dosage, duration of treatment, type of inhalation device, and patient characteristics like age, disease severity, and adherence to treatment. The review included 25 randomized controlled trials involving 8,471 children with mild to moderate persistent asthma. These trials compared daily ICS use (administered via various inhalation devices) to placebo or non-steroidal drugs over treatment periods ranging from three months to six years. Six different ICS molecules were studied: beclomethasone dipropionate, budesonide, ciclesonide, flunisolide, fluticasone propionate, and mometasone furoate, all administered at low or medium daily doses. The analysis revealed that ICS use was associated with a statistically significant reduction in linear growth velocity during the first year of treatment. Specifically, children treated with ICS experienced a mean reduction of 0.48 cm per year in growth velocity (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.65 to -0.30 cm/year) and a mean reduction of 0.61 cm in height from baseline (95% CI: -0.83 to -0.38 cm/year). These findings were based on moderate-quality evidence. Subgroup analyses indicated that the degree of growth suppression varied significantly between the six ICS molecules. However, no statistically significant differences were observed based on daily dose (low vs. medium), type of inhalation device, or the age of the child. The growth-suppressive effects of ICS appeared to be most pronounced during the first year of treatment and diminished in subsequent years. For example, during the second year of treatment, no significant difference in growth velocity was observed between ICS-treated children and controls (mean difference [MD]: -0.19 cm/year, 95% CI: -0.48 to 0.11 cm/year, P = 0.22). In the third year of treatment, results were mixed. One trial involving 667 participants found no difference in growth velocity between the budesonide and placebo groups (5.34 cm/year in both groups). However, another trial with 1,974 participants reported a lower growth velocity in the budesonide group compared to the placebo group (MD: -0.33 cm/year, 95% CI: -0.52 to -0.14 cm/year, P = 0.0005). Data on growth after discontinuation of ICS treatment were limited. Among four trials that reported post-treatment growth, three found no significant catch-up growth in the ICS group within two to four months after stopping treatment. One trial reported accelerated growth velocity in the fluticasone group 12 months after treatment cessation, but a significant height deficit of 0.7 cm remained between the fluticasone and placebo groups at the end of the three-year trial. A long-term follow-up study into adulthood found that prepubertal children treated with budesonide (400 μg/day) for an average of 4.3 years had a mean reduction of 1.20 cm in adult height compared to those treated with placebo (95% CI: -1.90 to -0.50 cm). In conclusion, regular use of ICS at low or medium doses is associated with a modest but statistically significant reduction in linear growth velocity and height during the first year of treatment in children with mild to moderate persistent asthma. The effect appears to be more strongly influenced by the specific ICS molecule than by the dose (within the low to medium range) or the type of inhalation device. Growth suppression is most pronounced during the first year of therapy and diminishes in subsequent years. Further research is needed to better understand the molecule-specific effects of ICS, particularly with newer agents like mometasone and ciclesonide, and to clarify the long-term impact of ICS on growth over several years of treatment.
